title: Working with directories - scandir, glob, mkdir, recursive delete safety
answer: scandir lists directory entries including . and .., which you usually skip. glob finds files matching a pattern, such as all *.php files. mkdir with recursive true creates nested folders in one call.
pitfall: Never build a delete path from user input without validation. A recursive delete on the wrong folder destroys data with no undo.

title: Reading files line by line and CSV - fopen, fgets, fgetcsv
keywords: file line by line kaise padhe
answer: Open a file with fopen, read it line by line with fgets, and always close it with fclose. fgetcsv parses one CSV row at a time so large files never need to be loaded fully into memory.
pitfall: Forgetting fclose leaks file handles, and on long-running scripts the process can run out of them. Close every handle you open, even on error paths.

title: Reading and writing files - file_get_contents and file_put_contents
answer: file_get_contents reads a whole file into a string, and file_put_contents writes a string to a file. Check file_exists first when a missing file is expected, and use LOCK_EX when several requests may write the same file at once.
pitfall: Passing a user-supplied filename straight to these functions allows path traversal, such as ../../etc/passwd. Validate the filename against an allow-list first.

title: File uploads - $_FILES, validation, and safe storage
answer: Uploaded files arrive in $_FILES with an error code, a temporary path, and a size. Check the error code, validate the real MIME type and extension against an allow-list, generate a new random filename, and move the file with move_uploaded_file into a folder outside the web root. This example is syntax-checked only because it needs a real HTTP upload.
pitfall: Trusting the uploaded filename or its extension lets an attacker upload a .php shell. Always rename the file and check the real MIME type.

title: JSON config files - json_encode, json_decode, and error checking
answer: Store configuration as JSON and read it with json_decode. Always check json_last_error after decoding, because a broken file returns null silently. Use JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR when you want a broken file to raise an exception instead.
pitfall: json_decode without the true flag returns objects, not arrays. Mixing the two styles in one codebase causes 'cannot use object as array' errors.
